title: Collect employees into a `Map<String, Set<String>>` (department → set of unique cities).
shortTitle: Collect employees into a Map<String, Set<String>> (department to set of unique cities)

s1_definition.profdef: You group by department and, within each group, map employees to their city collected into a set, using `groupingBy(dept, mapping(city, toSet()))`, giving each department its set of distinct cities.
s1_definition.analogy: For each department Priya lists the distinct cities its employees are based in — each city once.
s1_definition.oneliner: `groupingBy(dept, mapping(city, toSet()))` gives department to its set of unique cities.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You group by department and, within each group, map employees to their city collected into a set, using `groupingBy(dept, mapping(city, toSet()))`, giving each department its set of distinct cities.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** For each department Priya lists the distinct cities its employees are based in — each city once.

**One line to remember:** `groupingBy(dept, mapping(city, toSet()))` gives department to its set of unique cities.

sections.s2_technical:
`groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, mapping(Employee::getCity, toSet()))` buckets by department and, for each bucket, applies a mapping collector that extracts the city and collects into a set. The set deduplicates cities, so the value is the distinct cities per department, giving `Map<String, Set<String>>`.

The `mapping` downstream collector is the key: it transforms each element before passing it to a further collector, here toSet. Without mapping you would collect employees, not cities. The set removes duplicate cities automatically.

The senior nuance is composing a transforming downstream collector: mapping adapts the element to another type before the terminal collector, which is how you collect a derived value per group. I use toSet for uniqueness; for sorted unique cities I would nest `toCollection(TreeSet::new)`. I guard null department and city. This group-then-map-to-set pattern is common for building per-group distinct attribute sets.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A coverage report at the National Bank of India shows, per department, the distinct cities where it has staff.

This is exactly what groupingBy with a mapping-to-set downstream does — it collects the unique cities per department.

The code defines a `CoverageService.citiesByDepartment method and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: IT has Rajesh and Amit in Mumbai and Karan in Delhi; Sales has Priya in Mumbai.

Step 1: groupingBy buckets by department into IT and Sales.

Step 2: The mapping downstream extracts each employee's city within the group.

Step 3: toSet collects the cities, so IT's two Mumbai entries collapse to one, leaving Mumbai and Delhi.

Step 4: Sales has just Mumbai, giving the final map of department to distinct cities.

```
INFO: IT → [Mumbai, Delhi]
INFO: Sales → [Mumbai]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  [Rajesh/IT/Mumbai, Amit/IT/Mumbai, Karan/IT/Delhi, Priya/Sales/Mumbai]
    │ groupingBy(dept, mapping(city, toSet))
    │ IT: {Mumbai, Mumbai, Delhi} → {Mumbai, Delhi}  (dedupe)
    │ Sales: {Mumbai}
    ▼
  {IT=[Mumbai, Delhi], Sales=[Mumbai]}
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — groupingBy + mapping + toSet ═══

  ┌─ per-group distinct attribute set ─────────────────────────┐
  │ groupingBy(dept, mapping(city, toSet()))                    │
  │ mapping: transform element (→ city) before downstream       │
  │ toSet: dedupe cities per department                        │
  │ result: Map<String, Set<String>>                           │
  │ sorted unique → mapping(city, toCollection(TreeSet::new))   │
  │ guard null dept/city                                        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │            CoverageService    │
  │  + citiesByDepartment(List): Map │ group(dept)+mapping(city, toSet)
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. groupingBy(dept, mapping(city, toSet()))
  2. Map<String, Set<String>>
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To build a map of department to its set of distinct cities I group by department and use a mapping downstream collector that extracts the city and collects into a set. The mapping collector is the key: it transforms each element — here from an employee to its city — before handing it to the further collector, and toSet then deduplicates the cities so each department's value is its distinct cities. At the National Bank of India this backs a coverage report showing where each department has staff.

Without the mapping step I would be collecting employees rather than cities, so mapping is what adapts the element to the derived value I actually want per group. The set removes duplicate cities automatically.

The senior point I stress is composing a transforming downstream collector. mapping lets me project each element to another type before the terminal collector, which is the general way to collect a derived attribute per group. I use toSet for plain uniqueness, and when I need the cities sorted as well I nest toCollection with a TreeSet supplier instead. I guard null department and city so they do not create stray keys or entries. This group-then-map-to-set shape is a clean, reusable pattern for per-group distinct attribute sets.
